name: vol
one_line: Volatility 3: analyse memory dumps (also run as vol3, volatility3 or vol.py)
plain: A memory dump is a copy of everything that was in a computer's RAM at one moment. `vol` (Volatility 3) reads that dump and rebuilds what the operating system was doing: running processes, open network connections, loaded DLLs, command lines, passwords in memory, and more.

You run one plugin at a time, such as windows.pslist or linux.bash, with -f naming the dump. Volatility 3 finds the right symbols for the operating system itself (it may download them, so a lab may need them pre-installed).
In CTFs and incident response it answers: what was running, what was it connected to, and what did the attacker type or leave behind?
when: List the processes in a memory image.
See network connections at capture time.
Dump a process or a file from memory.
Read command lines, history and registry keys.

examples.title: What kind of image is it?
examples.explain: Shows the Windows version, build and kernel details. If this works, symbols are found and other plugins will work too.

examples.title: List processes
examples.explain: Prints PID, parent PID, name and start time. Look for odd names, wrong parents (cmd.exe from a Word process) and processes in strange paths.

examples.title: Process tree
examples.explain: Same data as a tree, so parent-child relations are easy to see.

examples.title: Find hidden processes
examples.explain: psscan scans raw memory for process structures, so it also finds processes that were unlinked from the normal list. Compare with pslist.

examples.title: Command lines
examples.explain: Shows the full command each process was started with, often revealing the attacker's tool and arguments.

examples.title: Network connections
examples.explain: Lists connections and listeners with owning process and addresses.

examples.title: Dump a process's files in memory
examples.explain: -o sets the output folder. Saves the files that process had mapped so you can analyse them with strings, file and exiftool.

examples.title: Check for injected code
examples.explain: Looks for memory regions that are executable and not backed by a file on disk, a classic sign of injected code.

examples.title: Linux image: bash history
examples.explain: Reads the bash history from memory. Linux images need a matching symbol table for the kernel.

examples.title: Search memory with strings
examples.explain: Not a Volatility plugin but often the fastest first look in a CTF.

options.plain: Output style: quick, pretty, csv, json, jsonl.
Treat the file as one location.
Basic system and process listing plugins.
Write files and process memory to disk.
Linux processes, shell history, open files, sockets.

mistakes: Running windows plugins on a Linux image: check the OS first with windows.info or banners.
Missing symbol tables: with no internet vol cannot analyse the image. Install symbols into the symbols folder first.
Trusting pslist alone: always compare with psscan.
Forgetting -o and dumping files into the current folder.
Wanting Volatility 2 profiles: Volatility 3 does not use --profile.
try: Run windows.info, pslist and pstree on a sample image and sketch the tree.
Compare pslist and psscan and look for a process that appears in only one.
Dump one process's files and run strings on them.
Write down the IP and port of every non-system connection in netscan.
see_also: strings(1), exiftool(1), binwalk(1), file(1), foremost(1), and the Volatility 3 plugin list with vol --help.
captured_with: Examples are written to explain a technique; they are not captured output.
